newsitem.title: USA: Foreign crude business to the U.S. stilled.
newsitem.headline: Foreign crude business to the U.S. stilled.

text.p: Foreign crude business to the U.S. was quiet Tuesday, despite what many traders see as improving economics for bringing physical North Sea barrels to the U.S. Gulf.
Traders said the volatility in the crude futures markets, due to the tensions in the Middle East between Iraq and the United States, has crept into the wet side of the business.
"It's just been so choppy out there, a lot of people really got whipsawed," said one New York trader, noting the quiet state of the market.
Players do however expect to see increased offerings of Norwegian and Brent due to the opening arbitrage.
The spread between November West Texas Intermediate and Brent stood at around $1.10-$1.20, and combined with a weak dated Brent value, make sense for selling to the U.S.
There were no wet Brent deals seen Tuesday, with the last trade still the extremely weak Monday sale at dated minus 47 cts to October Brent.

On the paper side, Brent spreads improved slightly during the U.S. session, trading at plus 58 cents for December/January. October/November was talked around 52 cents, and the November/December at around a 50 cents mark.
Outright November paper Brent sold for partial cargoes at $21.69 a barrel, 4 cents below the November IPE settle.
Other foreign talk was muted as well. Traders said they saw only sporadic dealings from Latin America.
On Monday, traders confirmed a Colombian Vasconia trade at WTI minus $1.90 FOB for October 10-14.
Last week, a Cano Limon parcel was sold at WTI minus $1.57 for October 3-7 to a Wall Street refiner.
